subject: Critical Thinking
title: Simpson's Paradox: Data That Lies When Combined
description: A 60-second lesson on Simpson's Paradox: Data That Lies When Combined.

hook.text: UC Berkeley was sued for gender bias in admissions. The overall data showed bias. But every department favored women.

buildup.text: Simpson's Paradox: a trend that appears in several groups reverses when the groups are combined.

discovery.text: Women applied to competitive departments with low admission rates. Men applied to easier ones. Aggregating hid this.

twist.text: A drug can be better for men AND better for women individually, but worse for the combined population.

climax.text: Simpson's Paradox shows that aggregated data can tell the exact opposite story from disaggregated data. Both are 'true.'

punchline.text: The data doesn't lie. But the summary might.

quiz.question: What is Simpson's Paradox?
options: A trend that appears in groups but reverses when groups are combined
A statistical error caused by small samples

details.summary: Simpson's Paradox occurs when a trend that appears in several different groups reverses when the data are combined. A treatment can help men and help women yet appear to hurt patients overall when the groups are merged.
details.whyItMatters: Simpson's Paradox shows that aggregated data can tell the opposite story from disaggregated data, making proper statistical analysis essential for correct conclusions.
takeaways: Combining data from subgroups can reverse apparent trends
Always check whether subgroup analysis changes the conclusion

faq.question: What is a famous real-world example of Simpson's Paradox?
faq.answer: UC Berkeley's 1973 admissions data appeared to show gender bias against women overall, but department-by-department analysis showed women were admitted at equal or higher rates. Women applied to more competitive departments, creating the false appearance of bias.

faq.question: How can you protect yourself from Simpson's Paradox when reading data?
faq.answer: Always ask whether the data combine different subgroups. Check if the pattern holds within each group separately. If the trend reverses at the subgroup level, the aggregate number is misleading and should not be used for decisions.
